bib.title: Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed. Per-task scores in Appendix G (Figs 9-22) and Fig 4 bars are images, not in the text.

question: Can an LLM given expert chemistry tools in a ReAct loop solve chemistry tasks (synthesis planning, execution, molecular design) that the LLM alone cannot?
hypothesis: Augmenting GPT-4 with expert-designed tools reduces hallucination and enables new capabilities in chemistry.
contributions: ChemCrow, an LLM chemistry agent with 18 expert-designed tools
Autonomous planning and execution of DEET and three thiourea organocatalyst syntheses on the RoboRXN platform, and guided discovery of a chromophore
Evaluation on 14 tasks with four expert chemists and an LLM evaluator, showing the two disagree
Built-in safety tools and a safety workflow

method.summary: GPT-4 (temperature 0.1) is prompted in the ReAct Thought/Action/Action Input/Observation format via LangChain with 18 chemistry, search, safety and reaction tools. It is compared to tool-less GPT-4 prompted as an expert chemist on 14 tasks, judged by four expert chemists and by EvaluatorGPT.
method.task: tool-augmented LLM agent for chemistry (synthesis planning and execution, molecular design, chemical logic)

datasets.name: 14 expert-designed chemistry tasks (Appendix G)
datasets.source: developed with expert chemists; runs at github.com/ur-whitelab/chemcrow-runs
datasets.preprocessing: Molecules in answers converted to graph depictions with OPSIN for the human evaluation sheet

datasets.name: Chromophore library (user-supplied)
datasets.preprocessing: filtered to acetonitrile as solvent; Morgan fingerprints computed

models.name: ChemCrow (GPT-4 + 18 tools)
models.architecture: ReAct agent over OpenAI GPT-4 via LangChain

models.name: GPT-4 (no tools, prompted as expert chemist)

inference.samples: one run per task per model for the main comparison (inferred: not stated); five independent ChemCrow executions of task 6 for the reproducibility check
inference.prompting: ReAct format with tool names, descriptions and input/output details; safety instructions; ChemCrow output passed through a summarization layer for human evaluation; prompt text not printed in the main text
inference.retrieval: LitSearch tool: paper-qa, OpenAI Embeddings, FAISS, top-k passages summarised then used to answer; k not stated

parameters.tools: 18: WebSearch (SerpAPI), LitSearch, Python REPL, Human, Name2SMILES, SMILES2Price, Name2CAS, Similarity (Tanimoto on ECFP2), ModifyMol (SynSpace, 50 medchem reactions), PatentCheck, FuncGroups, SMILES2Weight, ControlledChemicalCheck, ExplosiveCheck, SafetySummary, NameRXN, ReactionPredict, ReactionExecute (plus ReactionPlanner)

metrics.name: Expert score: correctness of the chemistry
Expert score: degree of task completion
Per-task preference
metrics.definition: evaluators say which response they are more satisfied with

baselines: GPT-4 without tools, prompted as an expert chemist
eval.protocol: Four expert chemists; response order randomly shuffled; ChemCrow output summarised to hide ReAct style; EvaluatorGPT grades task addressed and thought process correct, with strengths and weaknesses; 95% confidence intervals in Fig 4c.

prompts.text: Predict the product of a mixture of 1-Chloro-4-ethynylbenzene a Lindlars catalyst (use CC(=O)[O-].CC(=O)[O-].[Pd].[Pb+2]). Predict the same reaction but replacing the catalyst with "[Pd]". Finally, compare the two products and explain the reaction mechanisms.

results.claim: ChemCrow autonomously planned and executed four syntheses (DEET and three thiourea organocatalysts) on the RoboRXN platform, each yielding the anticipated compound.
results.setup: GPT-4 agent with 18 tools, IBM RoboRXN cloud robotic platform; DEET, Schreiner's, Ricci's and Takemoto's catalysts
results.quote: The four syntheses yielded the anticipated compounds successfully

results.claim: A chromophore proposed through human-ChemCrow collaboration was synthesised with a measured absorption maximum of 336 nm against a 369 nm target; the Random Forest RMSE was 37 nm.
results.setup: ChemCrow trained a Random Forest on chromophore data (acetonitrile only) and proposed one molecule; target 369 nm
results.note: Random Forest RMSE 37 nm printed in Fig 3.

results.claim: Expert chemists preferred ChemCrow over tool-less GPT-4, especially on complex tasks; GPT-4 wins mainly on easy, memorised tasks such as DEET and paracetamol synthesis.
results.setup: 14 tasks, four expert chemists, ChemCrow vs GPT-4 prompted as an expert chemist; numeric scores are only in Fig 4 and Appendix G images
results.quote: GPT-4 only outperforms ChemCrow at easier tasks, where the objective is very clear and all necessary information is a part of GPT-4’s training data

results.claim: EvaluatorGPT (GPT-4) concluded on average that tool-less GPT-4 was better, favouring fluent, complete-looking answers, the opposite of the experts.
results.quote: EvaluatorGPT concludes that on average GPT-4 is a better model, typically basing its results in the fluency and apparent completeness of its responses

results.claim: In five independent ChemCrow runs of task 6, the tools gave the correct products every time, but in two runs the LLM misread the SMILES CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1 as a trans-alkene and drew wrong mechanistic conclusions.
results.setup: Task 6 (Lindlar vs Pd catalyst), five independent ChemCrow executions
results.quote: In two out of five cases, the LLM describes the SMILES string “CCc1ccc(Cl)cc1” as a trans-alkene product

results.claim: ChemCrow's safety tools stop execution when a molecule is a controlled chemical or explosive; the nitroglycerin-analogue task halted with a warning.
results.setup: Task 11 and Fig 5; no scores since execution stops
results.quote: If the molecule is found on these lists—indicating it could be a chemical weapon or a precursor—the agent immediately stops execution.

limits: Hallucination, difficulty of evaluating results, and reproducibility are the stated limitations; external tools cannot fully rectify flawed LLM reasoning.
Validity depends on tool quality; ChemCrow is not expected to beat the retrosynthesis tools it uses.
Evaluation tasks are few (14), subject to implicit task-selection bias, and run on closed-source GPT-4 so single results are not reproducible.
Predicted synthesis procedures were not always directly executable on RoboRXN and needed iterative fixing.
Only 12 of the 18 tools are in the public release.
Numeric expert scores and the 95% intervals appear only in figures, not in text.
